description_full: Noble Corporation plc operates as an offshore drilling contractor for the oil and gas industry worldwide. It provides contract drilling services through its fleet of mobile offshore drilling units. The company also operates drilling rigs, such as floaters and jackups. It serves its fleets in Africa, the Far East Asia, the North Sea, the Oceania, South America, and the United States Gulf of America. Noble Corporation plc was founded in 1921 and is headquartered in Houston, Texas.

culture_narrative: Employs approximately 4K people. Revenue per employee of $730K ranks in the below the sector median among Energy peers, with revenue growing 32%/yr across its filed history. Each employee generates $96K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $7K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 4× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (1/10).
financial_summary: Noble Corporation plc A is a mid-cap energy business with a $6.2B market cap on $3.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +32% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 8% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $432M in free cash flow — roughly 13 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 4.39× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 3.6× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and thin 2.6× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 5.5% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 21% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

Operating margins softening -1.2pp YoY — early warning on the moat
Priced near or above estimated fair value, so the margin of safety has been bid away

Elevated short interest (12.5% of float) — sophisticated money is betting the other way
The commodity cycle — revenue and free cash flow are ultimately hostage to a price the company does not set, and the long-run energy-transition arc adds a structural overhang.
ESG-driven capital flight and stranded asset risk — tightening climate policy and investor mandates raise the cost of capital and risk leaving reserves permanently in the ground.
Geopolitical supply shocks — wars, sanctions, and OPEC decisions create volatility that no hedging programme can fully neutralise.

sect: Its 13% operating margin is roughly in line with the Energy median (16%).
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.16x).
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+49.4% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.05 across 203 companies in the universe; the top four hold 40% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 55% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 14% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 29% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 44% and a beta of 1.03, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.61 vs 5y 1.05), so read it loosely.
About $48.2M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 38% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $38.07 (margin of safety -2%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 0%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $8.89 to $120 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks expensive against Energy peers: P/E 118.2 vs 13.0 and EV/EBITDA 8.8 vs 6.8 (sector median).
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 6.9% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.3% (vs the 8% bar).
The 12 covering analysts target $47.17 on average, 21% above the price.
The price implies 14.6% annual cash-flow growth, 2pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 8% falls short of the cost of capital of 9.1%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.47).
It converts 13% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 4.39x.
ROE of 5% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.7x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.9% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 3.6x net debt to EBITDA ($471.4M of cash against $2.0B of debt), and interest cover is thin at 2.6x.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 32.5% over 3 years, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 33%).
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.00, a backlog worth 3% of annual revenue and deferred revenue down 8%.
It has missed earnings estimates by 115.3% on average.
own: Insiders own 20.7%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 88%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (15 sales, net $19.5M sold).
It returns 5.5% a year to shareholders (0.3% in buybacks and 5.1% in dividends).
The share count has grown 21.5% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It pays out 606% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
Short interest is elevated at 12.5% of the float, 10.2 days to cover.
people: With about 4,500 employees, each generates about $730K of revenue, 0.4x the Energy median, and revenue has grown 32.5% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $96K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.1M (4x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
